newsitem.title: USA: Fla. plaintiffs build case on smoke, disease.
newsitem.headline: Fla. plaintiffs build case on smoke, disease.

text.p: Until smoking was banned on U.S. flights, tobacco residue would build up so badly on aircraft wires, walls and other components that it would coat workers' hands and at times even affect cabin pressure systems, a former aircraft maintenance worker testified Wednesday.

"We used to have to clean it with a couple of cans of aerosol and throw water on it," Billy Jack Williams, a retired aircraft mechanic and electrician, said in a landmark flight attendants' lawsuit against the tobacco industry.
"It smelled like tobacco, and if you got it on your hand, (your hand) smelled like tobacco, and it was hard to wash off," he said.
Williams said he worked for National Airlines in the 1970s and Pan American World Airways from 1980 to 1991. Congress banned smoking on domestic flights in 1990.

He was called as a witness for plaintiffs in Norma Broin et al vs. Philip Morris Cos. Inc. et al, a $5 billion class action lawsuit brought against the tobacco industry by flight attendants who say they were sickened by breathing secondhand cigarette smoke on board U.S.-based aircraft.
Now in its third week of testimony, the trial in Dade County Circuit Court is the first class action and first secondhand smoke lawsuit against major cigarette companies to come before a jury.

During his testimony, Williams described how workers would remove aircraft wall panels and find tobacco residue coating bundles of wires, and said it also would build up on sensors and in outflow valves in some cabin pressurization systems.
"It was kind of a... residue-type thing. You could feel it, you could observe it, you could smell it," he said.
Earlier Wednesday, a cardiologist testified that years of research had convinced him that exposure to secondhand, or environmental, tobacco smoke, made non-smokers sick.

"I don't think there is any significant controversy about whether the effect is there, that is that secondhand smoke causes heart disease," said Dr. John Holbrook, a cardiologist and chief of the Division of General and Internal Medicine at the University of Utah School of Medicine.

By Wednesday the plaintiffs' attorneys, Stanley and Susan Rosenblatt, had called about a third of some 40 witnesses on their list, although they have said they will not call all of them. The trial began with jury selection June 2.

During cross-examination, David Hardy, an attorney for Philip Morris and Lorillard Inc., questioned Holbrook closely about when he felt comfortable saying that secondhand smoke causes heart disease. He cited Holbrook's comment that he had been convinced by a major study of the effect of secondhand smoke on nurses released this spring.
"Until May 1997, as far as you, Dr. Holbrook, were concerned, there was a real scientific controversy as to whether environmental tobacco smoke causes coronary heart disease?" Hardy asked.
Holbrook said he disagreed with Hardy's wording.

"Up until earlier this year, I considered environmental tobacco smoke to be a major risk factor. And that's a semantic that may not be easily appreciated by those outside the field, but it's a development of increasing evidence. ... It's not as if I suddenly changed my mind," he said.
The defence did not cross-examine Williams.
After the plaintiffs rest, attorneys for the nine tobacco defendants -- seven companies and two industry trade groups -- will begin calling their witnesses, who also number about 40.
The tobacco defendants say the incidence of lung cancer and other ailments among the flight attendants was no greater than that of other groups of non-smokers.
